lessons.title: The art of small talk
lessons.description: Turn a simple hello into a real conversation.

sections.title: Start with something you share
sections.body: Small talk helps people feel comfortable. Start with the place you are in, the weather, or an activity you share. Try saying 'This is a lovely classroom' or 'How was your weekend?'

sections.title: Keep the conversation going
sections.body: Ask an open question. Instead of 'Do you like books?', try 'What kind of books do you enjoy?' Listen to the answer and ask one more question. Share a little about yourself too.

sections.title: Try it with a partner
sections.body: Say hello to a classmate. Ask about their favourite food, a place they want to visit, or something they did yesterday. Spend two minutes listening before you switch roles.

lessons.question: Which question is most likely to start a longer conversation?
options: What do you enjoy doing after class?
lessons.explanation: An open question invites the other person to share more than a yes or no answer.

lessons.title: Everyday habits, simple sentences
lessons.description: Talk about the things you do, day after day.

sections.title: Meet the present simple
sections.body: Use the present simple for habits and facts. 'I walk to school.' 'They study English.' With he, she, and it, add -s or -es. 'She reads every morning.' 'He watches films.'

sections.title: Questions and negatives
sections.body: Use do or does to ask a question. 'Do you like music?' 'Does she play tennis?' Use do not or does not for a negative. 'I do not drink coffee.' After does, use the base verb without -s.

lessons.question: Choose the correct sentence.
lessons.explanation: With she, add -s to the verb in the present simple.

lessons.title: Your next stop
lessons.description: Useful phrases for finding your way in a new city.

sections.title: Ask for directions
sections.body: Begin politely. 'Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the station?' Useful direction words include straight ahead, turn left, turn right, next to, and opposite.

sections.title: Check you understood
sections.body: Repeat the key information. 'So I turn left at the cafe?' If you need help, say 'Could you repeat that, please?' Thank the person before you leave.

lessons.question: What does 'opposite the library' mean?
lessons.explanation: Opposite means on the other side, facing something.

lessons.title: Reading between the lines
lessons.description: Find the meaning that a writer leaves unsaid.

sections.title: Look for clues
sections.body: Writers do not always tell you everything directly. Read this sentence. 'Mia looked at the dark clouds and put an umbrella in her bag.' We can infer that Mia thinks it might rain.

sections.title: Use evidence
sections.body: An inference is a conclusion based on clues. It is different from a random guess. Look for actions, descriptions, and word choices that support your idea. Ask yourself what you know and what the text shows.

lessons.question: 'Leo checked his watch three times while waiting.' What can you infer?
options: Leo is probably impatient or worried about time.
Leo is learning to tell time.
lessons.explanation: Repeatedly checking a watch suggests that time matters to Leo in this moment.

lessons.title: Make your point
lessons.description: Share an opinion and support it with a reason.

sections.title: Say what you think
sections.body: Try phrases such as 'In my view', 'I would argue that', and 'From my perspective'. Then give a clear reason. 'In my view, reading fiction is valuable because it helps us understand other people.'

sections.title: Disagree thoughtfully
sections.body: Show that you heard the other person's idea. 'I see your point, but I think...' or 'That is an interesting argument. Have you considered...?' A good discussion helps both people learn.

lessons.question: Which phrase introduces a respectful disagreement?
options: I see your point, but I think...
lessons.explanation: Acknowledging the other person's point helps keep the discussion respectful.

lessons.title: One word, many possibilities
lessons.description: Build your vocabulary through word families.

sections.title: Meet a word family
sections.body: Words often belong to a family. Think of create, creative, creativity, and creation. They share a central meaning, but their roles in a sentence differ. Create is a verb. Creative is an adjective. Creativity and creation are nouns.

sections.title: Notice the ending
sections.body: Endings can give you clues. Many nouns end in -tion or -ity. Many adjectives end in -ful or -ive. Learn a word with its family and write one sentence for each form.

lessons.question: Which word is an adjective?
lessons.explanation: Creative describes a person or thing, so it is an adjective.
